Maladaptive Strategies.value: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I feel isolated and set apart from others
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination/feeling dirty is much more characteristic of sexual trauma than a mugging/robbery. In a robbery case it is not impossible, but without any corroborating interpersonal violation, bodily disgust, or related threat/memory content, this item is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me
issues.explanation: Emotional closeness as a trigger is difficult to link to the stated trauma type of mugging/robbery and to the rest of the profile. The other triggers, threat items, and memory content point to danger/safety and coercion themes, whereas this item implies an intimacy/interpersonal-betrayal theme that is not represented elsewhere.

vignette:
It had been six months since the night a man in a hooded jacket had pressed something hard into Priya's ribs behind a gas station, demanding her wallet and the keys to her delivery scooter. She had handed them over without a word, frozen, watching his face only as a blur of jawline and the glint of a streetlamp on what might have been metal. What stayed with her now was not the image of his face-she could not conjure it-but the sudden, suffocating wave of helplessness that would wash over her without warning, sometimes while she was standing in line for coffee, sometimes while she was lying in bed. The memory came as a snapshot: the cold pressure, the smell of damp asphalt, and then the sound of his voice, low and flat, which she would hear in her head at odd moments, as if it were playing on a loop she could not turn off.

Priya had been certain, in the weeks afterward, that she should have done something-kicked, screamed, run. She could not shake the belief that her paralysis meant she had failed herself, and that failure proved something fundamental about her: she was the kind of person bad things happened to, and there was nothing she could do to stop them. This conviction had settled into her chest like a stone. She began to feel isolated from everyone around her, as though the event had cut a thread connecting her to ordinary life, and she could no longer pretend she was safe the way other people were.

Driving became unbearable. As a delivery driver, Priya spent her shifts scanning the sidewalks for anyone who moved too quickly or stood too still, her eyes flicking from rearview mirror to side mirror, mapping every possible exit from the street she was on. She could not relax even when she was parked in a well-lit lot; her body stayed wired, waiting. At night she would wake at two or three in the morning, heart hammering, and get up to check the locks on her apartment door, even though she knew they were secure. She had started smoking cannabis most evenings to take the edge off, telling herself it was just to sleep, though she knew, somewhere beneath that thought, that the real reason was to stop the replaying of that night in her head. Sometimes, when the fear got too loud, she would tell herself it had not really happened-that she was overreacting, that the memory was not as bad as she thought-but the words never landed.

The more she avoided driving, the more her route planner at work started assigning her shorter, residential shifts, and the less money she made. But even the short routes felt dangerous now. Every time she saw a police car, her stomach dropped; she had come to associate authority with the moment after the mugging, when she had stood shaking on the curb and an officer had asked her, twice, whether she had gotten a good look at the man. She had not. She had not done anything. The guilt flared again, hot and familiar, and she would find herself scanning the street for escape routes, certain that something bad was about to happen again. What frightened her most was the way her own body seemed to have its own memory, flooding her with the full emotional intensity of the event even when she was not thinking about it-standing at a red light, or watching a customer approach her car, her heart would lurch before her mind had caught up.

Last week, she had pulled over mid-shift and called her supervisor to say she was sick, then sat in the driver's seat for twenty minutes, unable to move, planning how she would get out if someone tried to open her door. That was when she finally called a clinic. She was afraid of what would happen if she kept going like this-afraid she would lose her job, afraid she would never feel safe again, and most of all afraid that the voice in her head was right, and that she really was the kind of person who could not stop bad things from happening.
